title: Lesson 1.8: Privacy and physical security
use: Lesson 1.8 page in the Whop course. Hand-written gold-standard script: identity-linking chain, exchange-withdrawal/name-service/social-post exposure, wrench-attack risk and separated multisig as the structural fix, then home/device discretion. Facts last checked: 2026-09-26.

scenes.title: Privacy and physical security
scenes.sub: Keep your holdings private, and your household safe, as your on-chain wealth grows.
scenes.vo: Lesson one point eight. Privacy and physical security. By the end, you'll know how an address gets linked to your identity, and how to structure your keys so no single person can ever be forced to move everything.

scenes.vo: Here's the plan. First, why a public ledger means privacy is something you have to actively protect. Second, the real physical risk this creates, and the one structural fix that actually works. And third, the quieter habits, at home and on your devices, that back it up.

lines: to a mistake or a scam.
scenes.sub: It's about what happens when someone else can see how much you have.
scenes.vo: Every earlier lesson in this module protected you from losing funds to a mistake, a scam, or a bad contract. This one is different. It protects you from what happens when other people can see how much you have.

scenes.title: A public ledger
scenes.vo: A public ledger.

scenes.sub: Link an address to a name once, and its whole history is visible from then on.
scenes.vo: Start with the trade-off. The same public ledger that lets anyone verify a transaction also lets anyone who links an address to you see its full balance and history. Not just today's balance. Every transaction it has ever made, and every one it makes from now on.

scenes.title: How an address gets linked to you

nodes.label: Name service
nodes.sub: Easy to remember, easy to find

scenes.vo: Here's how that link actually gets made. Say you withdraw from an exchange. That exchange already knows who you are, because it collected your I.D. when you signed up. The moment you withdraw, it records which address received the funds. Separately, maybe you register an easy-to-remember name for that same address, or you post it publicly asking for a donation or showing off a trade. Any one of those, on its own, connects your name to that address. And once it's connected, every future transaction from that address is now readable as yours.

scenes.q: What does linking an address to your identity reveal?
scenes.a: Its full balance and history, now and every transaction it makes from now on.
scenes.vo: Quick check. What does linking an address to your identity actually reveal? [[pause 4]] The answer: its full balance and history, both what's there now and everything it does from that point on.

lines: addresses and attach names to them.
scenes.sub: Built to be readable, by design. That cuts both ways.
scenes.vo: And it isn't just other individuals who can make that link. Chain-analysis firms exist specifically to cluster addresses and attach names to them, and they sell that service to exchanges and investigators. None of this requires anyone to break in anywhere. It's all sitting on a ledger that was built to be readable by design.

scenes.title: Link less
scenes.sub: Separate what's public from what's savings.
scenes.vo: Link less.

scenes.title: Three habits that keep you unlinked
items: Never post addresses, screenshots, or wins publicly
One address for anything public, a separate one for savings
Treat any exchange-withdrawal address as already semi-public
scenes.vo: So the habit is simple: link less. Don't post addresses, screenshots, or wins publicly. Keep a separate address for anything public, a donation link, an N.F.T. you show off, and a completely different one for savings you never mention. And remember that any exchange withdrawal already links your I.D. to whichever address receives it, so treat that receiving address as semi-public too.
scenes.cap: So the habit is simple: link less. Don't post addresses, screenshots, or wins publicly. Keep a separate address for anything public, a donation link, an NFT you show off, and a completely different one for savings you never mention. And remember that any exchange withdrawal already links your ID to whichever address receives it, so treat that receiving address as semi-public too.

scenes.title: One mistake, and its fix

left.label: What Alex did
items: Posted a win, address visible
Balance and future moves now public
One key could move everything

right.label: The fix
items: No screenshots, ever
A vault address never shared publicly
Multisig: no single key is enough

scenes.vo: Here's the difference this makes, as one real comparison. Alex posts a screenshot of a big win, address visible in the corner. Anyone can now see Alex's balance, and follow every future move: a target has been created. The fix costs nothing: no screenshots, a vault address that has never once been shared, and, as you'll see next, a multisig so no single key can move it.

scenes.title: Roughly how identities get linked on-chain
scenes.vo: Put a rough shape on it. Across real cases of people getting doxxed on-chain, exchange withdrawals are usually the biggest source, because I.D. is already attached. Public posts and screenshots are the second biggest, and they're the one source that's entirely within your control. Name services and on-chain analysis make up the rest.
scenes.cap: Put a rough shape on it. Across real cases of people getting doxxed on-chain, exchange withdrawals are usually the biggest source, because ID is already attached. scenes.title: Two ways to operate day to day

left.label: Reused everywhere
items: One address for every swap and payment
Every link makes the next one easier
A single leak exposes the whole pattern

right.label: Fresh where it doesn't need to persist
items: A new address for anything one-off
Fewer links for anyone to draw
One leak exposes far less

scenes.vo: One more habit worth naming: address reuse. Using the same address everywhere, for every swap, every deposit, every payment, makes every one of those chain-analysis links easier to draw. A fresh address for anything that doesn't need to persist costs nothing and quietly removes most of the pattern.

scenes.title: Physical risk
scenes.sub: When the target isn't your wallet. It's you.
scenes.vo: Physical risk.

lines: Coercion, in person, for one signature.
scenes.sub: No smart contract stops this. Only how you've structured your keys does.
scenes.vo: Here's the risk that makes this lesson different from the rest of the module. Criminals have specifically targeted people known to hold crypto, in person, to coerce them into signing a transaction. In this industry it's bluntly called a wrench attack, and it's real enough that it shapes how serious holders structure their keys.

scenes.kicker: Low profile isn't enough on its own
lines: A low profile can still fail.
The real fix has to work anyway.
scenes.sub: It has to hold even if someone already knows you hold crypto.
scenes.vo: Low profile is the first defence, and it's just everything from the last section: no posts, no screenshots, no visible balance. But a low profile can fail. Someone talks. Someone guesses. So the real defence has to work even if you've already been identified.

scenes.title: A 2-of-3 multisig, held apart

nodes.label: Key 2: elsewhere
nodes.sub: A family member, a separate location

nodes.label: Any 2 of 3 sign
nodes.sub: Funds move. One coerced key, alone, cannot.

scenes.vo: That real fix is a multisig with keys held in separate physical locations. Say it's set up two of three. One key lives with you. One lives with a family member, or in a safe deposit box, somewhere else entirely. One lives with a lawyer or a trusted third party. No single key can move funds alone; any two of the three have to agree. Which means no single person, including you, under coercion, can be forced to move everything. The other key holders simply aren't there to sign.

scenes.title: Setting up a separated vault
steps: Pick 3 holders or locations that genuinely couldn't collude
Set up a 2-of-3 vault on an established contract (e.g. Safe)
Distribute one hardware device to each holder's own location
Test with a small amount before moving real savings in
scenes.result: Only after a successful small test does real savings move in
scenes.vo: Setting this up is a few concrete decisions, not new software you have to learn. First, pick three people or places that genuinely couldn't collude, not two family members who live together. Second, set up the vault as a two of three, using an established, audited multisig contract; Safe is the most widely used one in this space. Third, physically distribute a hardware device to each key holder's own location. And fourth, test it first with a small amount, before you ever move real savings into it.

stats: signature needed to drain a single key (illustrative)
separate people an attacker would need to coerce in a 2-of-3 (illustrative)
scenes.vo: One illustrative way to see why this matters. A single key gives an attacker exactly one target, and one signature ends it. A two of three vault, keys genuinely apart, gives an attacker three separate targets, none of which is enough alone. The defence isn't a bigger lock. It's removing the one moment where a single “yes” is sufficient.

scenes.q: How does multisig help against physical threats?
scenes.a: No single person can be forced to move everything; the other required keys are elsewhere.
scenes.vo: Quick check. How does multisig actually help against a physical threat? [[pause 4]] The answer: no single person can be forced to move everything, because the other keys needed to approve the transaction are somewhere else, held by someone else.

scenes.title: Home and devices
scenes.sub: The quieter habits that back all of this up.
scenes.vo: Home and devices.

scenes.title: What actually leaks a home setup
items: Discussing holdings with people who don't need to know
A hardware wallet or backup left somewhere visible
An unencrypted device that's also a stolen key
scenes.vo: Don't tell people who don't need to know. Keep your hardware wallet, and any written backup, out of sight. Not in a drawer a houseguest could open, and not photographed “for safekeeping.” Encrypt your devices, so a stolen laptop or phone isn't also a stolen seed phrase.

lines: None of this is a smarter contract.
It's how you arrange people and habits.
scenes.sub: Arranged before anything goes wrong, not improvised after.
scenes.vo: Notice the pattern across this whole lesson. None of it is about a smarter contract, or a better exchange. It's entirely about how you've arranged people, places and habits, before anything goes wrong. That's what makes it work even when a low profile has already failed.

scenes.title: The full setup, in order
steps: Keep the vault address unlinked, never posted or shared
Split vault custody 2-of-3, keys in separate locations
Store hardware wallet and backups out of sight, encrypted
Don't discuss holdings with anyone who doesn't need to know
scenes.result: No single point of failure: not a leak, not a device, not a person
scenes.vo: So here's the practical setup, start to finish. Keep your operating wallet's balance modest and your vault address unlinked. Split custody of the vault two of three, keys in separate locations. Store the hardware wallet and any written backup out of sight, encrypted where possible. And simply don't discuss your holdings with anyone who doesn't need to know. None of that requires new software. It's entirely how you structure what you already have.

scenes.q: What links your identity to a wallet address?
scenes.a: For example, a KYC exchange withdrawal, a name service, or posting the address publicly.
scenes.vo: Last check for this lesson. Name one thing that links your identity to a wallet address. [[pause 4]] The answer: an exchange withdrawal that already has your I.D. on file, a name service, or simply posting the address publicly.

scenes.title: The checklist
items: Savings addresses never posted or linked publicly
No holdings or wins posted on social media
Vault keys held so no single person can move everything
Backups stored discreetly, away from casual search
scenes.vo: Before your turn, here's the checklist version of everything you just saw. Have your savings addresses never been posted or linked publicly. No holdings or wins on social media, ever. Vault keys held so no single person could move everything alone. And backups stored discreetly, somewhere a casual search wouldn't find them.

scenes.sub: 5 to 15 minutes. Do it before you need it, not after.
scenes.vo: Your turn, five to fifteen minutes. Check every address you've ever posted, and stop posting new ones. Confirm your vault address has never been shared. And if you don't already have a split-custody vault, write down who would hold each key, and where, before you need it.

scenes.title: Three things to remember
items: Privacy is protected, not automatic, on a public ledger
Separated multisig holds even under physical coercion
Discretion at home backs up everything else
scenes.vo: To recap: a public ledger means privacy is something you protect, not something you get by default. Physical risk is real, and low profile alone isn't enough; separated multisig is the fix that holds even under coercion. And the quiet habits at home, discretion, encryption, out of sight, back all of it up.
That's privacy and physical security. Next up, Lesson one point nine: smart accounts and account abstraction, where your wallet itself gets programmable rules.
